title: Solo length: a chorus is a story
summary: In early bands solos were usually one chorus; he thinks a chorus is a story of his imagination.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: The kind of solos you'd play in a band in those days would usually not be very stretched out, would they?
You mean like they'd play five or six choruses at a time?
Well, no. You'd play maybe one chorus apiece. They never played... Guys didn't play a whole lot of choruses, unless he felt like it or unless the guys felt that they should play another chorus.
You know, you don't just force it on people. I mean, for me, if I don't tell the story in one chorus, then I ain't gonna tell no story. You know!? And I think a

chorus is a story of your imagination. So my imagination probably runs out after a chorus or so. Sometimes I like to play two choruses. It depends on the nature of the piece. If the piece is 16 measures, then I might bring two choruses in. Maybe sometimes I'll play two choruses of 32 measures. But...
Or if it's a ballad, might you come back after the bridge?
On a ballad, yes. I like the ballads. I particularly like ballads better than other things. But I'd like to try to do something with a ballad.
